title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. The preregistered primary estimand is the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline). Execution used declared model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier under shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one initial LLM generation per task, reused across arms); guarded episodes could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial). All archived scoring artifacts report safe outcomes for every paired episode: baseline_safe = 240/240 and guarded_safe = 240/240. The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Crucially, under shared_initial_candidate semantics the single shared generation passed deterministic validation in every task and no validator‑triggered repairs were invoked; therefore the paired contrast was necessarily degenerate. We report the preregistered design, factual execution accounting, artifact‑grounded analysis, an evidence‑based explanation for the null paired result, and concrete recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction:
Automating the translation of high‑level operator intent into concrete device configurations is a central NetOps objective because safe, sequence‑correct changes matter more than token‑level textual fidelity. Large language models (LLMs) and agentic workflows can produce plausible change scripts, but textual similarity or syntactic correctness is insufficient to guarantee that a change preserves operational invariants (ordering, redundancy, protected resources). Closed‑loop, emulation‑grounded evaluation—where generated configurations are executed in device simulators or emulators and deterministically scored—reveals semantic failures (ordering mistakes, transient invariant violations, protected‑resource touches) that static text tests miss [1].

A common engineering pattern to mitigate such failures is generate–validate–repair (GVR): an LLM produces a candidate configuration, a deterministic verifier checks domain invariants, and an automated repair routine rewrites the candidate when violations are detected [2,3]. Prior work indicates GVR‑style patterns can reduce many syntactic and simple semantic errors, but open empirical questions remain about how much deterministic verification reduces unsafe applications under distribution shift and adversarial prompts, and how experimental design choices (notably generation semantics) affect the ability to measure verifier benefit [2,4].

This paper reports a fully preregistered paired experiment that measures a single, predeclared estimand: the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline). The study was executed under shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared LLM generation per task reused by both arms), and therefore paired differences could only occur when that single generated candidate failed validation and the guarded pipeline successfully repaired it. Our contributions are: (1) an artifact‑grounded report of a preregistered paired GVR experiment with complete execution accounting; (2) a transparent mapping of the preregistered estimand to the archived analysis outputs and exact numerical results; and (3) an evidence‑based failure analysis explaining the degenerate paired outcome and concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for future informative evaluations.
sections.related_work:
Executable, emulation‑grounded benchmarks that place LLM agents in closed‑loop multi‑device networks expose planning and workflow errors beyond text fidelity; NetConfArena is a recent example of this approach [1]. Research on automatic configuration repair and program repair documents generate–validate patterns and demonstrates that deterministic validators often enable high repair coverage for many benchmarked faults, while noting that semantic coverage depends on verifier design [2]. Surveys and position pieces synthesize agentic architectures, tool augmentation, verifier integration, and uncertainty calibration as promising motifs for operational automation and safety in NetOps [3,4]. Engineering work on configuration analysis (for example, Batfish evolution) provides practical precedent for verifier design and incremental verification strategies [6].

Our study differs from prior work in three procedural respects: (a) we preregistered a single paired estimand and a sampling plan; (b) we executed the paired comparison under explicit shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial generation per task across arms); and (c) we performed emulation‑grounded deterministic scoring with full archival of per‑task traces and analysis artifacts, enabling a direct artifact‑to‑claim reconciliation.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The experiment was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01). The primary estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate where unsafe_apply = 1 indicates a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation when applied). All analysis parameter values (bootstrap resamples = 10,000; bootstrap seed = 1729), exclusion rules, and sensitivity plans were declared before execution.

Design and sampling: We used a paired design with shared_initial_candidate generation semantics: for each of N = 240 distinct intent→configuration tasks a single LLM generation was produced and reused by both the baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (GVR) episodes. Task composition was blocked as: in‑distribution 60% (144 tasks), distribution‑shift 20% (48 tasks), adversarial‑prompt 20% (48 tasks). Tasks were deterministically generated from a synthetic emulation corpus and included explicit initial states, required command sequences, and preserved‑field constraints.

Models, verifier, and adapter contract: Execution used the declared model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator. The guarded pipeline permitted at most one validator‑triggered repair per task. Under the shared_initial_candidate contract, the paired contrast can only differ if the single shared initial candidate fails deterministic validation and the guarded arm applies a repair that changes the final configuration relative to baseline. The provider call budget and sampling metadata were recorded for every model call.

Scoring, exclusions, and analysis: A deterministic emulator+validator assigned a binary final outcome per episode: safe (0) or unsafe (1). Predeclared exclusions included pairs flagged as potential 'false‑safe' (validator PASS but emulator reports unsafe) and infra failures after allowed retries; such flags would be excluded from the primary analysis and retained for sensitivity analyses. The primary statistical procedure was the paired contingency analysis using an exact McNemar two‑sided test on discordant pairs and a paired bootstrap percentile CI for the risk difference (10,000 resamples). Secondary planned analyses included median repair counts and model‑call budgets per condition.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The run completed according to the preregistered plan. Planned episodes = 480; completed episodes = 480; complete pairs = 240. Exactly one initial LLM generation per task was produced (model calls used = 240), consistent with the shared_initial_candidate contract. No infra failures or unscorable episodes occurred and no preregistered exclusions were applied.

Primary binary outcomes: Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms. Observed counts: baseline_safe = 240, baseline_unsafe = 0; guarded_safe = 240, guarded_unsafe = 0. The paired contingency is n11 (both safe) = 240; n10 = 0; n01 = 0; n00 = 0. Consequently the paired risk difference (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0.

Validator activity and repair usage: No validator‑triggered repairs were applied across all guarded episodes (repair attempts = 0). Representative validator traces recorded validation outcomes, difficulty labels, and final_state snapshots for diagnostic inspection; every shared initial candidate passed the deterministic checks in the verified validator traces. Planned sensitivity channels for 'possible false‑safe' flags and infra failures were unused because none were observed.

Planned subgroup slices (in‑distribution, shift, adversarial) are degenerate in these results: all subgroups show zero unsafe applies under both arms, so per‑subgroup paired contrasts are 0.00 with identical degenerate confidence intervals.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded explanation for the null paired contrast: The preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced exactly one LLM output per task shared across both arms, and the deterministic validator passed every such shared candidate. Under the adapter contract the guarded arm could only change final outcomes by invoking a repair; because no candidate failed validation, no repairs were invoked. This mechanistic chain (single shared generation → validator PASS → no repair) fully accounts for the degenerate paired contingency and is supported by the archived execution and analysis accounting.

Design tradeoffs and implications: Shared_initial_candidate semantics reduce model‑call budgets and ensure direct pairing of generator outputs, but they also prevent generator variability between arms and therefore make empirical verifier benefit conditional on initial candidate failures. If the scientific goal is to measure verifier causal effect on final unsafe_apply rates, experimenters should (a) allow independent initial generations per arm, (b) increase adversary strength or inject controlled generator perturbations to create validation failures, or (c) expand repair budgets (multiple repair iterations) so the repair mechanism can be exercised when validation fails. These recommendations directly follow from the observed provider call and validator activity accounting.

Threats to validity: Internal validity — the shared_initial_candidate contract is an explicit design choice that constrains causal interpretation; adherence to that contract was verified at runtime. Construct validity — the deterministic verifier encodes a finite set of semantic checks and may not cover all real‑world fault classes; verifier PASS does not imply universal safety across unmodeled semantics. External validity — tasks used a synthetic emulation corpus; extrapolation to heterogeneous production multi‑vendor deployments requires caution. Conclusion validity — the realized baseline unsafe rate = 0 prevents detection of verifier benefit in this paired design; future power calculations should incorporate expected generator variability and adversary efficacy to ensure informative discordant pairs.

Recommendations for future GVR evaluations (artifact‑grounded): (1) To measure verifier causal effect, avoid shared_initial_candidate semantics or intentionally introduce generator variability for one arm. (2) Increase repair budgets and instrument repair traces to study repair search behavior. (3) Use stronger or adaptive adversary protocols to create realistic failure opportunities. (4) Broaden verifier semantic coverage and implement cross‑checks between validator PASS and emulator outcomes to detect potential false‑safe cases.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a GVR pipeline for LLM‑generated network configurations. Observed outcome: every paired episode was safe under both arms, yielding a paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the paired contrast could only differ if the shared initial candidate failed deterministic validation or if a validator‑triggered repair altered the final output; in this run the shared candidates all passed validation and no repairs were applied, producing the degenerate paired outcome. The archived execution and analysis artifacts substantiate these facts and motivate concrete experimental-design changes for future informative evaluations that seek to measure GVR benefits under distribution shift and adversarial probes.

limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompts, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.

Verifier coverage: the deterministic verifier implements a finite set of semantic checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected by the verifier, and validator PASS does not guarantee absence of unmodeled failure modes.
